title: C is for CONTROLLED AIRSPACE: How to fly through invisible walls without fear | MSFS A-Z
description:
Picture this: You're cruising along a completely clear sky. No stop signs, no concrete barriers, and nothing but open air ahead. But the truth is, you're flying through invisible walls. Cross these lines in the real world without permission, and you could get your license revoked or even find yourself intercepted by military jets. If you're flying on networks like VATSIM or using built-in air traffic control, crossing these boundaries unannounced is the fastest way to ruin a controller's day.

Welcome back to Microsoft Flight Simulator A to Z! In this episode, we are demystifying the sky with the letter C for Controlled Airspace. If you've ever avoided using ATC or felt too intimidated to log onto VATSIM because you don't know where you are legally allowed to fly, this video is your ultimate cheat code. We break down the alphabet soup of airspace classes—Alpha to Golf—using simple, real-world analogies so you can completely eliminate radio anxiety. Finally, we jump right into the cockpit for a live flight demonstration, showing you exactly how to read these floating boundaries on your moving map and how to execute the precise radio calls needed to cross them safely.

In this video, you’ll discover:

The Airspace Alphabet: A breakdown of Class Delta, Charlie, Bravo, Alpha, Echo, and Golf using clear, practical analogies.

The Two-Way Rule vs. Explicit Clearance: Why simply talking to ATC is enough for a Class Charlie, but will get you a violation in Class Bravo.

Navigating the EFB and Maps: How to overlay airspace boundaries on your moving map and read critical ceiling and floor limits.

Live ATC Transition Demo: Step-by-step communication inside Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 to request flight following and clear a Class Charlie transition seamlessly.

🕒 Chapters
00:00 - Intro
01:03 - Class Delta
01:38 - Class Charlie
02:07 - Class Bravo

04:43 - Demo: the radio call

Understanding the invisible rooms in the sky separates casual simmers from real-world virtual pilots. Before your next flight, map out your route, check your airspace floors, and ensure you know exactly who to call before crossing the line.
